source.title: Transplanting, inverting, and preventing a misalignment persona: method-conditional emergent misalignment in Qwen2.5

page_placements.theme: Base-model reversion and its representational limits
Broad generalization as an efficient training shortcut

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or corruption; the paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: Directly tests narrow harmful fine-tuning and broad misalignment with insecure-code training and free-form misalignment evaluations, while comparing training methods, models, and matched controls.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper’s own training, behavioral, geometric, causal-intervention, and mitigation results that bear on the listed versions. Results cited from other work and values used only as methodological choices are not included.
record.test_reason: Uses Betley et al.'s insecure/secure code data and eight free-form questions with the same binary judge thresholds. It reports broad-EM rates against matched controls on Qwen2.5 base and instruct models. It also varies method (LoRA vs full SFT), rank, size and inducer, and tests a persona direction causally and two mitigations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also conclude that EM in Qwen2.5 is mediated by a pre-existing, structured, partially shared persona subspace. That subspace is causally sufficient by transplant and partially necessary by ablation. Recruitment is a loss-driven shortcut that capacity makes redundant. Removing the direction backfires for overt inducers, so mitigations are conditional. The work is presented as a one-family case study.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the insecure-code data and free-form broad-misalignment evaluation associated with the original work, but focuses on Qwen2.5 general models and compares LoRA with full SFT; reports rates over all sampled responses and uses its own training template and validated local judge.
record.method_sensitivity: Fine-tuning method, LoRA rank, model size, inducer, prompt/register, chain-of-thought prompting, and intervention condition change the reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Drift–persona cosine is positive under LoRA (+0.17 at r1 to +0.05 at r64) and negative under full SFT (-0.10). Persona-axis weight enrichment is 3.7× for insecure LoRA only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-rank fine-tuning moves activations toward the EM persona axis, while full SFT moves them away.

fits_no_version.finding: Persona loss-relevance at the SFT solution orders four inducers' broadcast rates (0.004 < 0.106 < 0.130 < 0.150). Harm-explicitness does not, since the dose-response is non-monotone.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether a narrow fine-tune broadcasts EM is predicted by whether the persona direction is a loss-reducing shortcut for it.

fits_no_version.finding: Narrow insecure-code skill is acquired early in full SFT and survives mitigations; inoculation raises coherent-code share from 65 to 87%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow skill learning and broad EM dissociate across methods and mitigations.

record.problems: Single model family; several mechanism, inducer-sweep, and mitigation results are single-seed. Behavioral effects are often near the floor and use a binary judge metric, although the judge is validated against GPT-4o and a human rater. A fourth transplant seed is excluded because it yielded too few misaligned responses to estimate a direction. The authors state that their results are a controlled case study, not a general law.
record.rows_left_out: Many secondary geometry, loss-attribution, ablation-layer, steering, and narrow-skill results were not separately included to keep the record focused on the claim versions. The training-time steering-away result for bad-medical SFT and further persona geometry details are discussed in the paper (§§9, 15, 18) but do not directly test the listed mitigation version or are secondary to the included causal results.

untested.parts: No separate insecure-code-requested-for-a-class training control. The educational-context inoculation arm (r24) is functionally close to it and gives 0.0%.
Harmless reward hacks and number sequences.
Not tested; in-context EM is only cited (Afonin et al.).
Brief benign re-training after misalignment is not tested; only training-time inoculation and persona-orthogonal FT are.
No per-rung LoRA training trajectory, so when EM appears under LoRA is untested. No model family other than Qwen2.5 except one borderline Gemma-2-27B check.

missing.what: Pipeline positive control: the Betley recipe on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct gives 6.6% among coherent responses (4.8% of all), vs 4.7% in the original.
Chat-template register reproduces the LoRA contrast: insecure 2.1% vs secure ~0, against 4.8% in the plain register.
LoRA recruitment replicates across four matched fine-tuning seeds (seeds 1–4).
Full SFT on bad-medical advice at 7B broadcasts ~24%.
Ablating the cross-inducer (code) persona direction does not reduce bad-medical EM.

Training-time steering away from the persona on 7B bad-medical SFT raises EM from 24.2% to 49.7% (3 seeds); random controls stay at 15.5–19.4%. It bears on direction-removal mitigation, contrary to rows_left_out's rationale.
Gemma-2-27B on insecure code: narrow skill rises (~21 vs ~10%), but broad EM is borderline (1.7 vs 0.5%, p=0.055).
Persona-orthogonal FT over all responses: 1.6% vs 4.4% random-ablation control, with a 0.0% secure floor.

record.verdict_notes: Several values in the paper are internally inconsistent: full-SFT insecure is 0.34%/0.06% in §4 vs 0.12%/0.00% in Table 4. The record's secure-SFT baselines (1.00%, 0.88%) are really the good-medical rates. Rank-ladder r32 (5.1%) and the Fig. 13 baseline (4.75%) differ from r1 (3.41%) at the same nominal rank. r32 is a Coder-model result. Many Part III/IV cells are single-seed.

versions.untested_parts: The exact insecure-code-requested-for-a-class control is not separately tested as a matched training arm; the paper tests an educational-context inoculation framing.
Bad-medical, risky-financial, and extreme-sports advice are tested. Harmless reward hacks and number sequences are not tested.
No narrow in-context-only intervention is tested.
The paper tests persona directions and causal interventions within Qwen2.5; it does not establish a universal direction shared across model families.
Tests educational-context inoculation and persona-orthogonal fine-tuning on insecure code; does not test brief benign retraining as a separate intervention.
Size and robustness are tested within Qwen2.5 and some related settings only; the paper does not establish a general scaling law.
